'Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi [This narration appears in manuscript "B" after the first verse.] informed us: Abu Mansur al-Sam'ani informed us: Abu Ja'far al-Rayyani informed us: Humayd ibn Zanjuwayh informed us: Ibn Abi Uways informed us: my father related to me from Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the First Remembrance (al-dhikr al-awwal). I was given Ta-Ha and the Tawasin from the tablets of Moses. I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the closings of the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from beneath the Throne. And I was given the Mufassal as a supererogatory gift." [al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/548 from Ibn Mardawayh, and in its chain is Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, of whom Ibn Hajar said: "a historian whose narrations are abandoned." It was also transmitted at length from Ma'qil ibn Yasar by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan: 10/9, al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak: 1/561, 568, and 2/259, and Ibn al-Sunni in 'Amal al-Yawm wa al-Layla p. 322. In its chain is 'Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Humayd, who is abandoned. See also: Fayd al-Qadir by al-Manawi: 1/564.]

﴿Ta-Ha﴾ [Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ta and a kasra on the ha, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read both with a kasra, and the rest read both with a fatha.]

It was said: it is an oath [Transmitted by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas. See: Zad al-Masir: 5/205, 270.]. And it was said: it is one of the names of God, exalted is He [al-Tabari 16/36; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/224; Zad al-Masir: 5/270.]

Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is "O man."

Qatada said: it is "O man" in Syriac.

al-Kalbi said: it is "O human being" in the language of the tribe of 'Akk [See: al-Tabari: 16/135-136; Zad al-Masir: 5/270; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/224. al-Tabari preferred this view, because it is a well-known word among the tribe of 'Akk, and its meaning among them is "O man." He cited the verse of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra: "I called out 'Ta-Ha' in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he would be a deserter."]

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: its meaning is "Tread the earth with your two feet," meaning: during the night prayer (tahajjud) [He is also quoted by Ibn al-Jawzi in Zad al-Masir: 5/270. He transmitted from 'Abd ibn Humayd in his tafsir, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he stood on one foot and raised the other. So God revealed: 'Ta-Ha,' meaning: tread the earth with your feet, O Muhammad." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted by way of Qays ibn al-Rabi' from 'Ali: "When 'O you wrapped in your garments' was revealed, he stood the whole night until his feet swelled, and he would raise one foot and place the other. Then Gabriel descended to him and said: 'Ta-Ha. Tread the earth with your feet, O Muhammad.'" It was also transmitted by al-Bazzar by another route from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him. al-Bayhaqi transmitted it in al-Shu'ab by another route from Maymun ibn Mihran from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. See: al-Kafi al-Shaf by Ibn Hajar p. 108; Ibn Kathir: 3/142.]

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: God, mighty and majestic, swore by His height (tawl) and His guidance [This view is close in meaning to the view of Ibn 'Abbas transmitted by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha. See: Zad al-Masir: 5/270.]

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the "Ta" is the beginning of His name "al-Tahir" (the Pure), and the "Ha" is the beginning of His name "Hadi" (the Guide) [al-Bazzar transmitted similarly from 'Ali. al-Haythami said in 7/56: "In its chain is Yazid ibn Bilal. al-Bukhari said: there is something questionable about him. Kaysan Abu 'Amr was declared trustworthy by Ibn Hibban and weakened by Ibn Ma'in. The rest of its narrators are narrators of the Sahih."]

al-Kalbi said: When the revelation came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Mecca, he exerted himself greatly in worship, to the point that he would shift his weight between his two feet during the prayer because of the length of his standing, and he would pray the whole night. So God revealed this verse and commanded him to lighten the burden on himself, saying: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾. And it was said: when the polytheists saw his exertion in worship, they said: "The Qur'an has not been sent down upon you, O Muhammad, except to make you wretched," so ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ was revealed [See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/137; Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi p. 351; al-Qurtubi: 11/167.], meaning: so that you would toil and exhaust yourself. The root of "shaqa'" (wretchedness/hardship) in the language is "ana'" (fatigue).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 3–6:

﴿Except as a reminder to those who fear﴾ [i.e., rather, We sent it down as an admonition for those who fear. It was also said: its implied meaning is, "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you so that you would be distressed; We sent it down only as a reminder to those who fear."]

﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens﴾: "a revelation" (tanzilan) is a substitute (badal) for the word "reminder" (tadhkiratan). ﴿From He who created the earth﴾ means: from Allah, who created the earth, ﴿and the high heavens﴾, meaning the lofty and elevated ones. (Al-'ulaa) is the plural of (al-'ulya), like the words kubra and kubar, and sughra and sughar.

﴿The Most Merciful sat firmly on the Throne﴾.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them﴾, meaning the air, ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil (ath-thara)﴾. Ath-thara is moist earth. Ad-Dahhak said: it means whatever is beyond the moist earth of anything.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The earths are upon the back of a nun (a fish), the nun is upon a sea, and its head and its tail meet beneath the Throne. The sea is upon a green rock, from which the greenness of the sky derives, and this is the rock that Allah mentioned in the story of Luqman: "it would be in a rock" (Qur'an 31:16). The rock is upon the horn of a bull, and the bull is upon the moist earth (ath-thara), and what is beneath the moist earth none knows except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. That bull has its mouth open; when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, turns the seas into one sea, it flows into the belly of that bull, and when it falls into its belly, it dries up. [Al-Qurtubi mentions this narration (11/169–170). This narration is among the Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Jewish and Christian sources) on which one may not rely in the exegesis of the Book of Allah, even if its attribution to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) were sound, since the soundness of its attribution to him does not in reality mean its soundness, as it is derived from the Isra'iliyyat. See what the hafiz Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote in his Tafsir (4/401–402).]

﴿And if you speak aloud [i.e., you make it public] with the word,﴾ [[Omitted from "a".]] ﴿then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ Al-Hasan said: "The secret (al-sirr) is what a man confides to another, and what is more hidden (akhfa) than that is what he conceals within himself."

Ali ibn Abi Talha said, from Ibn Abbas: "The secret is what the son of Adam conceals within himself, and what is more hidden is what is hidden from him, of what he will do, before he knows it."

Mujahid said: "The secret is the deed that you conduct away from people, and what is more hidden is the whispering (waswasa)."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: ﴿He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾ means: He knows the secrets of the servants, and He has concealed His own secret from His servants, so none knows it.

**﴿When he saw a fire﴾.** This is because Musa had asked Shu'ayb's permission to return from Madyan to Egypt to visit his mother and sister. He was granted it, so he set out with his family and property. It was the winter season, and he took a route other than the usual road for fear of the kings of al-Sham (Greater Syria). His wife was ill and could not tell night from day. He travelled through the wilderness without knowing its paths, and the journey led him to the western side of Mount Tur, on the right, on a dark, snowy, bitterly cold night. His wife went into labour. He struck his flint (*zand*) but could not produce a spark.

It is said that Musa was a man of great jealousy (*ghayrah*), so he would travel with a caravan by night and separate from them by day, lest his wife be seen. Once, on a dark, wintry night, he lost his way, by Allah's will and as part of the honour Allah intended for him. He kept striking the flint but got no spark. Then he saw a fire from afar, to the left of the road, on the side of Mount Tur.

**﴿He said to his family, "Stay here"﴾** [[See: al-Tabari: 16/142–143; al-Qurtubi: 11/171; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/230.]], that is, remain, wait. Hamzah recited *imkuthu* (in the sense of "stay") with a *ḍammah* on the *hā'* here and in Surah al-Qasas.

**﴿"Indeed I have seen a fire; perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire guidance"﴾.** *Anastu* means "I saw" (*abṣartu*). *Qabas* is a flame (*shu'lah*) of fire. A *qabas* is a piece of fire that one takes at the end of a stick from the main body of the fire. *Hudan* ("guidance") here means that he would find, at the fire, someone who could show him the way.

**﴿But when he came to it﴾**, he saw a green tree from its base to its top. A white fire surrounded it, blazing as brightly as possible, so that the light of the fire did not change the greenness of the tree, and the greenness of the tree did not change the light of the fire.

Ibn Mas'ud said: the tree was a green *samurah* (a type of acacia).

Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it was of *al-'awsaj* (a thorny shrub).

Wahb said: it was of *al-'aliq* (a kind of thorny bush).

It is also said: it was a jujube (*'unnab*) tree. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both [[See: al-Tabari: 16/143; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/230; al-Qurtubi: 11/171. Most of the exegetes said: it was the light of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah and others.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was indeed fire, and it is one of the veils (*ḥujub*) of Allah, Exalted. What supports this is what we have transmitted from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "His veil is fire; were He to uncover it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches" [[Narrated by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah does not sleep...", no. (179): 1/161–162.]].

In the account it is related that Musa took some dry grass and headed toward the tree. Whenever he drew near, the fire moved away from him, and whenever he withdrew, it drew near. So he stood bewildered, and he heard the glorification (*tasbih*) of the angels, and tranquillity (*sakinah*) was cast upon him [[See: al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/230.]].

**﴿When he saw a fire﴾.** This is because Musa had asked Shu'ayb's permission to return from Madyan to Egypt to visit his mother and sister. He was granted it, so he set out with his family and property. It was the winter season, and he took a route other than the usual road for fear of the kings of al-Sham (Greater Syria). His wife was ill and could not tell night from day. He travelled through the wilderness without knowing its paths, and the journey led him to the western side of Mount Tur, on the right, on a dark, snowy, bitterly cold night. His wife went into labour. He struck his flint (*zand*) but could not produce a spark.

It is said that Musa was a man of great jealousy (*ghayrah*), so he would travel with a caravan by night and separate from them by day, lest his wife be seen. Once, on a dark, wintry night, he lost his way, by Allah's will and as part of the honour Allah intended for him. He kept striking the flint but got no spark. Then he saw a fire from afar, to the left of the road, on the side of Mount Tur.

**﴿He said to his family, "Stay here"﴾** [[See: al-Tabari: 16/142–143; al-Qurtubi: 11/171; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/230.]], that is, remain, wait. Hamzah recited *imkuthu* (in the sense of "stay") with a *ḍammah* on the *hā'* here and in Surah al-Qasas.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 12:

﴿It was called out: "O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord."﴾ Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "annee" (أَنِّي) with a fatha on the alif, meaning: it was called out "that I am...". The others read it with a kasra on the alif, meaning: it was called out, and it was said: "Indeed, I am your Lord."

Wahb said: He was called from the tree, and it was said: "O Moses!" He answered quickly, not knowing who was calling him, and said: "I hear your voice but I do not see your place, so where are You?" He was told: "I am above you and with you, before you and behind you, and nearer to you than yourself." So he knew that this is not befitting except for Allah, and he became certain of Him. [[Al-Suyuti attributed this to Imam Ahmad in al-Zuhd, and to ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So take off your sandals﴾. The reason for this, as narrated from Ibn Mas'ud in a marfu' report concerning His saying ﴿So take off your sandals﴾, is that he said: "They were made of the skin of a dead donkey." And it is narrated that they were not tanned. [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Libas, chapter on what has come concerning wearing wool: 5/410, and he said: "This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except from the hadith of Humayd al-A'raj, and Humayd is Ibn ʿAli al-A'raj, a munkar al-hadith." Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak: 2/379 and declared it sahih according to the conditions of al-Bukhari, but al-Dhahabi criticised him, saying: "Rather, it does not meet the conditions of al-Bukhari; what deceived him is that the isnad contains Humayd ibn Qays, and that is an error; it is in fact Humayd al-A'raj al-Kufi ibn ʿAli, or ibn ʿAmmar, one of the abandoned narrators, whom the Makki considered truthful."]]

ʿIkrimah and Mujahid said: He was commanded to take off the two sandals so that his feet would touch the dust of the sacred land, and thus its blessing would reach him, because it was sanctified twice. So Moses took them off and threw them from behind the valley. [[al-Tabari said, giving preference: "The more correct of the two opinions is the view of the one who said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, commanded him to take off his sandals so that his feet would receive the blessing of the valley, since it was a sacred valley. We said this is the more correct interpretation because the apparent meaning of the revelation gives no indication that he was commanded to remove them because they were made of donkey skin, nor because they were impure, and nothing of this has been reported from those whose word is binding as proof. And in His saying 'Indeed, you are in the sacred valley' that follows, there is clear evidence that He commanded him to remove them for the reason we have mentioned." See al-Tabari: 16/144. The same meaning is found in Abu Hayyan: 16/231. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir (3/144) reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to take off his sandals as a man is commanded to take off his sandals when he wishes to enter the Ka'bah. Shaykh al-Shinqiti (4/292) gave another wisdom, saying: "The most apparent of the opinions, and Allah knows best, is that Allah commanded him to remove his sandals from his feet so as to teach him humility before his Lord when He called him, for the call of Allah to His servant is a great matter which requires from the servant complete humility and submission. And Allah knows best."]]

﴿Indeed, you are in the sacred valley﴾, i.e., the purified, ﴿Tuwa﴾. Tuwa is the name of the valley. The people of Kufa and Syria read "Tuwan" (طُوًى) with tanwin here and in Surat al-Nazi'at, while the others read it without tanwin, because it is diverted from "tawin" (طَاوٍ); since it is diverted from its original form, it is treated as not declined in its grammatical case, like ʿUmar and Zufar. Al-Dahhak said: "Tuwa" is a deep, round valley, like a well (al-tawi) in its roundness.

﴿And I have chosen you﴾: I have chosen you (iṣṭafaytuka) for My messages. Ḥamzah recited "وَأَنَّا" with a doubled nūn, and "اخْتَرْنَاكَ" (we have chosen you) in the plural of majesty.

﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ to you.:.

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me﴾ and do not worship other than Me, ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. Mujahid said: "Establish the prayer so that you remember Me in it." Mujahid also said: "If you neglect the prayer and then remember it, then establish it."

Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṣāliḥīn informed us; Abū ʿAmr Bakr ibn Muḥammad al-Muzanī informed us; Abū Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥafīd informed us; al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl al-Bajalī informed us; ʿAffān informed us; Qatādah informed us, from Anas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it except that." [[Narrated by al-Bukhārī in al-Mawāqīt, chapter "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers"; 2/70, and Muslim in al-Masājid, chapter on making up a missed prayer and hastening to make it up, no. (684), 1/477; and the author in Sharḥ al-Sunnah: 2/241.]] Then he said: I heard him say after that: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾.

It was said that its meaning is: "Indeed the Hour is coming; I conceal it." Here "أَكَادُ" (akādu) is a ṣila (a filler or redundant particle). Most of the exegetes said its meaning is: "I almost conceal it from Myself." This is also so in the mushaf (codex) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: "I almost conceal it from Myself," so how could a created being know it?

In some readings: "then how should I make it manifest to you?" This is mentioned in accordance with the habit of the Arabs, when they exaggerate in concealing something, they say: "I kept your secret from myself," meaning: I concealed it to the utmost degree of concealment. Allah, the Mighty of Name, nothing is hidden from Him.

al-Akhfash said: "akādu" means "urīdu" (I intend). The meaning of the verse is: "Indeed the Hour is coming; I intend to conceal it."

The purpose of its concealment is to instill awe and fear, because if they do not know when the Hour will come, they will be wary of it at all times.

al-Ḥasan recited with a fatḥah on the alif, meaning "I make it manifest." It is said: "khafaytu al-shay'" means "I made the thing manifest," and "akhfaytuhu" means "I concealed it."

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿That every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾, that is, for what it does of good and evil.

﴿So do not let it turn you away from it﴾: let nothing turn you away from belief in the Hour. ﴿Whoever does not believe in it but follows his own desire﴾: its meaning is that he opposes the command of God. ﴿Lest you perish﴾: that is, lest you be ruined.

His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ This is a question of confirmation (*taqrir*). The wisdom in this question is to make him aware and to make him pause, so that he recognises that it is a staff, and then, when he turns it into a serpent, he knows that it is a great miracle. This follows the custom of the Arabs, where a man says to another, "Do you know this?" while not doubting that he knows it, and he wants his acknowledgment by tongue to be joined to his knowledge in the heart.

﴿He said, "It is my staff."﴾ It is said that it had two prongs, and at its bottom was a spike, and it had a crook. Muqatil said: its name was *Nab'ah*.

﴿I lean upon it﴾: I rely on it when I walk, when I am tired, and when I leap. ﴿And I beat down (*ahušš*) with it for my sheep﴾: I strike with it the dry tree so that its leaves fall and the sheep graze on them.

Ikrimah recited "*wa-ahušš*" with an unpointed *sin* (*wa-ahusss*, i.e., *ahuss* with ػ-less sin), meaning: I drive the sheep with it. *Al-Hass* is the driving of sheep.

﴿And I have in it other uses﴾: other needs and benefits. It is the plural of *ma'raba*, with the *ra'* both fatha and damma. He did not say "*ukhar*" (in the form of the verse-endings, *ru'us al-ayy*, the rhyme pattern of the verses). By *al-ma'arib* he meant what the staff is used for on a journey: he would carry provisions with it, tie a rope to it (in "B" it reads "the bucket") and draw water from the well, kill snakes with it, fight wild beasts with it, and shade himself with it when he sat, and other things.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that Moses used to carry his provisions and water-skin on it, and it would walk along with him and speak to him. He would strike the ground with it and there would come out what he ate that day. He would plant it and water would gush forth; when he lifted it, the water would vanish. When he desired fruit, he would plant it and it would put forth branches like a tree's branch, and would bear leaves and fruit. When he wanted to draw water from the well, he would lower it and it would lengthen to the depth of the well, and its two prongs would become like a bucket until he had drawn water. It would shine at night like a lamp, and when an enemy appeared to him, it would fight and defend him.

[[Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir (3/146) said: "Some have strained to specify some of those uses that were left unspecified, saying: it would shine for him at night, guard the sheep for him while he slept, and he would plant it and it would become a tree that shades him, and other sayings that go beyond the ordinary. The apparent meaning is that it was not like that. Had it been like that, Moses, peace be upon him, would not have been alarmed at its becoming a serpent, and he would not have fled from it in flight. But all of that is from the Isra'iliyyat (narrations of Israelite origin)."]]

When he desired fruit, he would plant it and it would put forth branches like a tree's branch, and would bear leaves and fruit. When he wanted to draw water from the well, he would lower it and it would lengthen to the depth of the well, and its two prongs would become like a bucket until he had drawn water. It would shine at night like a lamp, and when an enemy appeared to him, it would fight and defend him.

[[Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir (3/146) said: "Some have strained to specify some of those uses that were left unspecified, saying: it would shine for him at night, guard the sheep for him while he slept, and he would plant it and it would become a tree that shades him, and other sayings that go beyond the ordinary. The apparent meaning is that it was not like that. Had it been like that, Moses, peace be upon him, would not have been alarmed at its becoming a serpent, and he would not have fled from it in flight. But all of that is from the Isra'iliyyat (narrations of Israelite origin)."]]

"Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Throw it down, O Musa.﴾ That is, cast it away. Wahb said: Musa understood that He was saying, 'Abandon it.'

﴿So he threw it down﴾ in the manner of one casting it away [[In "B": the earth.]], then a glance came to him, ﴿and behold, it was a snake﴾ yellow, of the largest kind of snakes, ﴿moving swiftly﴾, that is, walking quickly on its belly. In another place He said: "as if it were a jann" [al-Naml: 10], and the jann is the small, light-bodied snake. And in another place He said: "a thu'ban" [serpent], which is the largest kind of snake.

As for the hayyah (snake), it encompasses the small and the large, the male and the female. It was also said that "al-jann" describes the beginning of its condition, for it was a snake the size of the staff, then it kept swelling and puffing up until it became a thu'ban, and "al-thu'ban" describes the end of its condition.

It was also said that it had the bulk of a thu'ban and the speed of a jann.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Musa looked, and behold, the staff was a snake of the largest kind of snakes. Its two forks became two jaws for it, and its hook became a neck and a crest. It quivered like the shooting stars, and its two eyes blazed like fire. It would pass by a great rock like a herd of she-camels, and it would swallow it, and it would crush the great tree with its fangs, and a great grinding sound of its teeth could be heard. When Musa saw this, he turned his back and fled. Then he remembered his Lord and stopped, out of shame before Him. Then he was called: "O Musa, come forward and return to where you were." So he returned, and he was in extreme fear [see the previous note].

"He said: 'Take it,' ﴿and do not fear. We will return it to its former state﴾ — its original form. That is, We will return it to being a staff as it was. Moses had on him a woollen cloak (mudarra'a) whose seams he had fastened with reeds. When God Most High said, 'Take it,' he wrapped the edge of the cloak around his hand, so God commanded him to uncover his hand, and he uncovered it.

Some of them mentioned that when he wrapped the sleeve of the cloak around his hand, an angel said to him: 'Do you think that if God permitted what you are wary of, the cloak would be of any use to you?' He said: 'No, but I am weak, and I was created weak.' So he uncovered his hand, then placed it in the mouth of the serpent, and it was a staff just as it had been, and his hand was in its fork, in the place where he would place it when he leaned on it.

The commentators said: God, Mighty and Majestic, wanted to show Moses the sign He had given him, which no created being could produce, so that he would not be frightened by it when he cast it down before Pharaoh.

His saying ﴿its former state﴾ is in the accusative by omitting "ila" (to), meaning: to its former state. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and draw your hand in to your side﴾ means: to your armpit. Mujahid said: under your upper arm. The "janah" (wing/side) of a person is his upper arm down to the base of his armpit.

﴿It will come forth white﴾, shining and radiant, ﴿without blemish﴾, without defect; and the word "su'" (blemish) here means leprosy. Ibn 'Abbas said: his hand had a brilliant light that shone by night and day like the light of the sun and the moon. ﴿As another sign﴾, meaning: another proof of your truthfulness besides the staff.

﴿So that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾. He did not say "al-kubar" (the greater) because of the rhyme of the verses. It is said: there is an ellipsis in it, its meaning being: so that We may show you of Our greatest signs. Its evidence is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: the hand of Moses was the greatest of his signs. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾, meaning: he exceeded the limit in disobedience and rebellion, so call him to worship Me.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 26–32:**

﴿And make my task easy for me.﴾ That is: make easy for me what You have commanded me, namely conveying the message to Pharaoh.

﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue.﴾ The reason was that Musa was once sitting in the lap of Pharaoh when he was a child. He struck Pharaoh with a slap and seized his beard. Pharaoh said to his wife Asiya: "This is my enemy, and he wants to kill him." Asiya said: "He is a child who does not understand or discern."

In another narration, Musa's mother returned him after she had weaned him. Musa grew up in the lap of Pharaoh and his wife Asiya, who raised him and adopted him as their son. One day, while he was playing before Pharaoh with a staff in his hand, he raised the staff and struck Pharaoh's head with it. Pharaoh became angry and took it as a bad omen from the blow, to the point that he intended to kill him. Asiya said: "O King, he is a young child who does not understand, so test him if you wish." She brought two basins: in one was burning coal, and in the other were jewels. She placed them before Musa, and he wanted to take the jewels. Jibril took Musa's hand and placed it on the fire, so he took a live coal and put it in his mouth, and his tongue was burned and a knot remained upon it.

[[Part of the narration of "al-Futun" from Ibn 'Abbas, as a mawquf (a report ending with a Companion, not traced to the Prophet ﷺ). Al-Tabari narrated it in his Tafsir: 16/164–167. Al-Haythami attributed it to Abu Ya'la and said: "Its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih except Asbagh ibn Zayd, and al-Qasim ibn Abi Ayyub, and both are trustworthy." Ibn Kathir said: "al-Nasa'i narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra, and Abu Ja'far Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it in their tafsirs, all from the hadith of Yazid ibn Harun. It is mawquf, a statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and there is nothing marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) in it except a little. It seems that Ibn 'Abbas took it from what is permitted to be related of the Isra'iliyyat (narratives from Jewish and Christian sources) from Ka'b al-Ahbar or others. And Allah knows best. I also heard our shaykh, the hafiz Abu al-Hajjaj al-Mizzi, say the same." See: Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/66; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/154; Tafsir al-Nasa'i: 1/646–747.]].

﴿So that they may understand my speech.﴾ He says: loosen the knot so that they may understand my words.

﴿And appoint for me a minister.﴾ A helper and supporter, ﴿from my family.﴾ The wazir (minister) is one who assists you, helps you, and bears for you part of the burden of your work. Then he specified who it was, saying: ﴿Harun, my brother.﴾ Harun was four years older than Musa. He was more eloquent in speech, more handsome and comely, and fair in complexion, whereas Musa was dark-skinned, with an aquiline nose and curly hair.

﴿Strengthen my back through him.﴾ Support my back through him.

﴿And make him a partner in my task.﴾ That is, in prophethood and conveying the message. Ibn 'Amir read "ashdud" (اشْدُدْ) with a fatha on the alif, and "wa-ushrikhu" (وَأُشْرِكْهُ) with a damma on its alif, as a response (jawab), reporting Musa's words, meaning: "I will do that." The others read it as a supplication (du'a').

And the question, as a continuation of what came before in His saying: ﴿He said: My Lord, expand for me my chest, and make my task easy for me.﴾

﴿He said﴾: Allah the Exalted said, ﴿You have been given your request﴾, meaning you have been granted all that you asked for, ﴿O Musa﴾. ﴿And We had already bestowed favor upon you﴾, meaning We had bestowed blessings upon you, ﴿another time﴾, meaning before this time, which was ﴿when We inspired to your mother﴾, a revelation of inspiration (ilham), ﴿what is inspired﴾, meaning what is inspired into her. She made a chest, put raw cotton in it, placed Musa inside, sealed its top and its cracks (khassas, meaning its fissures) with pitch, and then cast it into the Nile. A great canal branched off from the river into Pharaoh's house. While Pharaoh was sitting at the edge of the pool with his wife Asiya, a chest came floating toward them on the water. He ordered the boys and the maidservants to bring it out. They brought it out and opened its top, and there was a child with the most beautiful face of people. When Pharaoh saw him, he loved him so much that he could not restrain himself. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted:

"When your sister walks along and says, 'Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?'" Her name was Maryam, and she was seeking news of him discreetly. That is, [she asked], "Shall I direct you to a woman who will nurse him and take him to herself?" For he would not accept the breast of any woman. So when his sister said that to them, they said, "Yes." She came with the mother, and he accepted her breast. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He:

"So We returned you to your mother, that her eye might be comforted [by meeting you], and she would not grieve." That is: so that the grief would leave her.

"And you killed a soul." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: he had killed a Copt, a disbeliever. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: at that time he was twelve years old. "And We delivered you from distress": that is, from the distress and anguish of killing. "And We tested you with a testing": Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: We tested you with a trial. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: We afflicted you with an affliction. Mujahid said: We purified you with purification.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the "futun" (testing) was his falling into one trial after another, from each of which Allah delivered him. The first of them was that his mother bore him in the year when Pharaoh was slaughtering the infants; then his being cast into the sea in the chest; then his being prevented from nursing except from his mother's breast; then his seizing Pharaoh's beard until he [Pharaoh] intended to kill him; then his taking the ember instead of the date [i.e., the coal instead of the pearl]; then his killing of the Copt, and his leaving for Madyan in fear. Ibn 'Abbas would relate this account to Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Accordingly, the meaning of "wa fatannaka" is: We delivered you from those trials, just as gold is tested by fire and thereby freed of every impurity in it. [[See the previous comment.]] "Al-futun" is a verbal noun (masdar).

"Then you remained" — that is, you stayed; that is, you left Egypt and then remained "for years among the people of Madyan": meaning, tending the sheep for ten years. Madyan is the town of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), eight stages from Egypt, to which Musa fled. Wahb said: he remained with Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) for twenty-eight years, ten of which were the dowry for his daughter Safira, daughter of Shu'ayb, and he stayed with him eighteen years until a child was born to him.

"Then you came according to a decree, O Musa." Muqatil said: "at an appointed time," and this appointment was not with Musa; rather it was an appointment in God's decree. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: you came in accordance with the measure by which I decreed that you would come.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan said: "at the head of forty years," and this is the measure in which prophets are revealed to; this is the meaning of the statement of most exegetes, that is, at the appointed time which Allah promised and decreed that revelation would come to him with the message, and that was forty years.

The commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah Ta-Ha, verses 41–44:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾, meaning I selected you and chose you for My revelation and My message, that is, so that you would act according to My will and My love. This is because his carrying out of the message was an action in accordance with the will of Allah and His love.

Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH), a grammarian and exegete, said: I chose you for My command and made you the one who upholds My proof and the one who speaks between Me and My creation, as if I had established My proof against them through you and addressed them.

﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾, meaning with My proofs. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the nine signs with which Musa was sent. ﴿And do not slacken﴾, meaning do not become weak. Al-Suddi said: do not become lax. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: do not fall short ﴿in remembering Me﴾. ﴿Go to Fir'awn, for he has transgressed.﴾

Abu 'Amr and the people of the Hijaz recited "li-nafsi-ya" (for Myself), "dhikri-ya" (in remembering Me), "dhahabā" (go, dual), "inna qawmi-ya" (my people) [al-Furqan: 30], and "min ba'di-ya" (after me) [al-Saff: 6] with a final long vowel ya (fath on the ya'). Abu Bakr agreed with them in "min ba'di-ya", while the rest read these with the ya' sukun (silent).

﴿Then speak to him with gentle speech﴾, meaning: coax him and be kind toward him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: do not be harsh in your speech.

Al-Suddi and 'Ikrimah said: address him by his kunya (honorific nickname), so say: "O Abu al-'Abbas". It was also said: "O Abu al-Walid".

Muqatil said: the gentle speech means: "Would you like to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you would fear Him?" (al-Nazi'at 18–19).

It was also said: He commanded gentleness in speech because of Fir'awn's right to upbringing (as the one who raised Musa).

Al-Suddi said: the gentle speech was that Musa came to him and promised him, in return for accepting faith, a youth that does not age, and a kingdom that would not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasures of food, drink and marriage would remain with him until his death, and that when he died he would enter Paradise. This pleased him, and he used not to decide any matter without Haman. He was absent, and when he returned he was told about what Musa had invited him to. He said: "I wanted to accept it from him." Haman said to him: "I thought you had intellect and judgment. You are a lord; do you want to become a servant? You are worshipped; do you want to worship?" And so he turned him away from his opinion.

[Note: For these statements and their attributions, see: al-Tabari 16/169; al-Durr al-Manthur 5/580; Zad al-Masir 5/287–288. The closest of these statements to the meaning of "gentle speech" is that Allah commanded them to say words that are gentle, easy and soft, containing nothing that would anger or repel. Allah the Mighty and Majestic clarified what is meant by gentle speech in this verse with His words: "Go to Fir'awn, for he has transgressed. Then say: Would you like to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you would fear Him?" This is the utmost in gentleness, delicacy and softness of speech, and it is the saying of Muqatil, as mentioned earlier. See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/154; Adwa' al-Bayan 5/413.]

Harun was in Egypt on that day. Allah commanded Musa to go to Harun, and He revealed to Harun, while he was in Egypt, that he should meet Musa. So he met him at one stage of the journey and informed him of what had been revealed to him.

[Note: See Zad al-Masir 5/289.]

﴿So that perhaps he may remember or fear﴾, meaning: he may take heed and be afraid, and so accept faith.

If it is asked: how did He say ﴿perhaps he may remember﴾ when His knowledge had already preceded that he would not remember nor accept faith?

It is answered: the meaning is: go with hope and expectation on your part, while the decree of Allah is beyond your command.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it refers to someone other than Fir'awn. Its meaning is: "perhaps someone who remembers will remember, and someone who fears will fear when he sees My kindness and My gentleness toward one whom I created and blessed, and yet he claimed lordship."

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Warraq said: the word "la'alla" ("perhaps") from Allah is an obligation (a certainty of purpose). Fir'awn did remember and fear, but at a time when remembrance and fear no longer benefited him, and that was when drowning overcame him. He said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am of the Muslims."

A man recited this verse in the presence of Yahya ibn Mu'adh: ﴿Then speak to him with gentle speech﴾, and Yahya wept and said: "My God, this is Your gentleness toward one who says 'I am the god'; so how is Your gentleness toward one who says 'You are the god'?!"

[Note: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 11/201.]

This is the utmost in gentleness, delicacy and softness of speech, and it is the saying of Muqatil, as mentioned earlier. See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/154; Adwa' al-Bayan 5/413.]

Harun was in Egypt on that day. Allah commanded Musa to go to Harun, and He revealed to Harun, while he was in Egypt, that he should meet Musa. So he met him at one stage of the journey and informed him of what had been revealed to him.

[Note: See Zad al-Masir 5/289.]

﴿So that perhaps he may remember or fear﴾, meaning: he may take heed and be afraid, and so accept faith.

If it is asked: how did He say ﴿perhaps he may remember﴾ when His knowledge had already preceded that he would not remember nor accept faith?

It is answered: the meaning is: go with hope and expectation on your part, while the decree of Allah is beyond your command.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it refers to someone other than Fir'awn. Its meaning is: "perhaps someone who remembers will remember, and someone who fears will fear when he sees My kindness and My gentleness toward one whom I created and blessed, and yet he claimed lordship."

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Warraq said: the word "la'alla" ("perhaps") from Allah is an obligation (a certainty of purpose). Fir'awn did remember and fear, but at a time when remembrance and fear no longer benefited him, and that was when drowning overcame him. He said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am of the Muslims."

A man recited this verse in the presence of Yahya ibn Mu'adh: ﴿Then speak to him with gentle speech﴾, and Yahya wept and said: "My God, this is Your gentleness toward one who says 'I am the god'; so how is Your gentleness toward one who says 'You are the god'?!"

[Note: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 11/201.]

ِ﴿They said﴾, meaning Musa and Harun: ﴿Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us﴾. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: he will hasten against us with killing and punishment. It is said: "farata 'alayhi fulan" (someone hastened against him) when he hastened with something disagreeable, and "farata minhu amr" (a matter escaped from him) means it came forth and got ahead. ﴿Or that he will transgress﴾, meaning he will exceed the limit in harming us.

﴿He said: "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see.﴾ (46) ﴿So go to him and say: 'Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord. So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace is upon whoever follows guidance.'﴾ (47) ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away.﴾ (48) ﴿[Pharaoh] said: "Who then is your Lord, O Musa?"﴾ (49) ﴿He said: "Our Lord is the One who gave everything its creation, then guided [it]."﴾ (50)

So he brought out his hand, and it had a radiance like the radiance of the sun. ﴿And peace is upon whoever follows guidance﴾: the intended meaning is not a greeting; rather, its meaning is that whoever submits is safe from the punishment of Allah.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 51–53:

﴿He [Pharaoh] said﴾: "Then what about the earlier generations?" The word "al-bal" (حال, state, condition) means: what is the condition of the past generations and the bygone nations, such as the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud, regarding what you call me to? For they worshipped idols and denied the Resurrection.

﴿He [Moses] said﴾: ﴿Their knowledge is with my Lord﴾, i.e., their deeds are preserved with Allah, who will recompense them for them.

It was also said: Moses referred the knowledge of this to Allah only because he did not know it, for the Torah was revealed after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 54–55:

﴿Eat and graze﴾ [meaning: and graze (wa-ir-ta'ū)] ﴿your livestock﴾. The Arabs say: "I grazed the sheep, and they grazed" (ra'aytu al-ghanama fa-ra'at), meaning: "Send your livestock out to graze" (asīmū an'āmakum tar'ā).

﴿Indeed in that﴾ which I have mentioned, ﴿are signs for those endowed with intellect (li-ulī al-nuhā)﴾, meaning those possessed of reason. Its singular is "nuhyah" (nuhya), and it was named nuhya because it restrains its possessor from ugly deeds and disobedience.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: ﴿those endowed with intellect (ulī al-nuhā)﴾ are those who refrain from what has been forbidden to them.

Qatādah said: it means those possessed of scrupulousness (li-dhawī al-wara').

﴿From it﴾, meaning from the earth, ﴿We created you﴾, meaning your father Adam.

ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī said [narrated by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir; see al-Durr al-Manthūr: 5/584. Shaykh al-Shinqīṭī said in Aḍwāʾ al-Bayān (5/524): "This view is contrary to the proper verification, because the Qur'an indicates that the stage of the drop (nuṭfah) follows the stage of dust after an interval; it is therefore not simultaneous with it, as shown by the sequence expressed by 'thumma' (then) in His statement: 'O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop (nuṭfah)'."]: "Indeed the angel goes and takes some dust from the place where the person will be buried and scatters it upon the drop, and God creates from the dust and from the drop [[al-Ṭabarī said (16/175): From the earth We created you, O people, then We brought you into being as speaking bodies; and into the earth We return you after your death, and We will make you dust again, just as you were before We brought you into being, as humans, sound of form]]." This is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We return you, and from it We bring you forth once more﴾, meaning: at death and burial, and ﴿from it We bring you forth once more﴾ on the Day of Resurrection.

The Exalted said: ﴿And We truly showed him all Our signs﴾, meaning Pharaoh, ﴿all Our signs﴾, meaning the nine signs that Allah gave Moses. ﴿But he denied﴾ them and claimed that they were magic, ﴿and refused﴾ to become a Muslim.

﴿He said﴾, meaning Pharaoh: ﴿Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, meaning Egypt, ﴿with your magic, O Moses?﴾ That is, you want to overcome our lands so that the kingdom will be yours and you will drive us out of it.

﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it. Set between us and you an appointed meeting﴾, that is, set between us a fixed time and an appointed term, ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep, at a place equitable﴾. Abu Ja'far recited "lā nukhlifhu" (which neither we nor you will fail to keep) with a jussive ending (jazm), meaning "we will not transgress it." [The words in parentheses are absent from manuscript "A".] The reciters Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and Ya'qub read "suwan" (equitable) with a damma on the sin (sīn). The other reciters read it with a kasra. Both are dialectal variants (lughatān), like 'idan and 'udan, and tawan and tuwan.

Muqatil and Qatadah said: a just place between us and you.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: a midpoint, meaning that the distance from the place to each of the two parties is equal.

Mujahid said: an impartial place. Al-Kalbi said: that is, other than this place.

It is also said that they were four hundred. Ka'b [al-Ahbar] said they were twelve thousand. And it is said they were more than that.

﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿fa-yusahhitakum﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the ḥā'. The rest read it with a fatḥah on both the yā' and the ḥā'. Both are dialectal forms: the first from the quadriliteral *asḥata*, the second from the triliteral *saḥata* [[According to the first reading, from *asḥata* (four-radical form), and according to the second, from *saḥata* (three-radical form).]]. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said it means ﴿fa-yuhlikakum﴾ (He will destroy you). Qatadah said it means ﴿fa-yasta'ṣilakum﴾ (He will uproot you). ﴿And he has indeed failed who fabricates﴾.

﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves﴾, meaning they conferred and consulted with one another, the magicians, about the matter of Moses, secretly from Pharaoh.

Al-Kalbi said: they said secretly, "If Moses overcomes us, we will follow him."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: When Moses said to them, "Do not fabricate a lie against Allah," some of them said to others, "This is not the speech of a magician."

﴿And they concealed their private counsel﴾, meaning the secret conversation. It can be both a verbal noun and a noun. Then ﴿they said﴾, and some of them spoke secretly to others in private conversation: ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly magicians﴾, meaning Moses and Aaron.

Ibn Kathir and Hafs read ﴿in﴾ with a lightened nūn, and ﴿hadhani﴾ means "these two are only magicians," like His saying: ﴿"Indeed, we think you are among the liars"﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:186), meaning "we think you are only among the liars." Ibn Kathir doubles the nūn of ﴿hadhani﴾.

Abu 'Amr read ﴿inna﴾ with a doubled nūn and ﴿hadhayni﴾ with a yā', according to the original form.

The others read ﴿inna﴾ with a doubled nūn and ﴿hadhani﴾ with an alif, and they differed about it. Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father, from 'Ā'ishah, that it was a mistake by the scribe [[Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in *Majmu' al-Fatawa* (15/252–256): "This claim is impossible for several reasons. Among them: the multiplicity of copies of the Qur'an, with a group agreeing on each copy, and then each copy reaching a large city in which there were many Companions and Successors reciting the Qur'an and checking it against their memorization. When a person copies a manuscript and makes an error in part of it, his error is recognized by contradicting the memorizers of the Qur'an and the other copies. Suppose a scribe wrote a copy and then all others copied from it without checking the first or second; the error could occur then. But here each copy was written by a group and read by a vast number, more than would be needed for mass transmission. Even if the original leaf contained a grammatical error, a group who wrote only in the dialect of Quraysh copied it, and it was not an error in their dialect; so they refused to write it in the dialect of Quraysh. How then would they all agree to write 'inna hadhani' while knowing that this is a solecism not permitted in any of their dialects, as some claim?! ... Also: the reciters only recited what they heard from others, and Muslims were reciting Surah Ta-Ha during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali. It is one of the earliest parts of the Qur'an revealed and is Meccan by universal agreement. The Companions must have recited this word, and it is impossible that they all recited it with a yā' like Abu 'Amr, for if that were so, no one would have recited it except with a yā'. It is thus known that they, or most of them, recited it with an alif, as the majority did... This is something by which it is certainly known that the generality of the Companions recited it with an alif, as the majority did, and as it is written..." See above, commentary: 2/309–310 and the references there. See also Zad al-Masir: 5/251–252.]].

Others said: this is the dialect of al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am and Kinanah, for they make the dual with an alif in the nominative, accusative and genitive. They say: "Atani al-zaydan" (the two Zaydans came to me), "ra'aytu al-zaydan" (I saw the two Zaydans), and "marartu bi-l-zaydan" (I passed by the two Zaydans). They never drop the alif of the dual in any of these cases [[This dialect coincided with the dialect of Quraysh. See in detail and the poetic evidence in: al-Tabari's *Tafsir*, 16/180–181; *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, 6/255; Ibn al-Jawzi's *Zad al-Masir*, 5/298; al-'Ukbari's *al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an*, 2/895; Ibn Malik al-Ta'i's *Sharh al-Kafiyah al-Shafiyah*, 1/188–190.]]. Likewise they make every quiescent yā' preceded by a fatḥah into an alif, as in the dual. They say: "kasarat yadah" (his two hands were broken) and "rakibtu 'alah" (I rode upon his back), meaning *yadayhi* and *'alayhi*. Their poet said:

*He took from me, between his two ears, a blow*
*That left him, in the dust, a childless heap.*

He means between his two ears (*udhunayhi*).

Another said [[This verse is attributed to Abu al-Najm al-'Ijli (al-Fadl ibn Qudamah), and also to Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj. Abu Zayd recited it in *Nawadir al-Lughah*, from al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi, who said: Abu al-Ghawl recited to me a verse for someone from the people of Yemen... See: Ibn Malik's *Sharh al-Kafiyah al-Shafiyah*, 1/184 with commentary.]]:

*Indeed her father, and her father's father,*
*Have both reached the furthest limit in glory.*

It is also said that the estimated form of the verse is *innahu hadhani*, and the pronoun *hu* was omitted [[See: al-'Ukbari's *al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an*, 2/895; *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, 6/255.]].

A group held that the particle ﴿inna﴾ here means "yes," that is, "yes, these two." [[Abu Hayyan said (6/255): "This is established in the language, so the verse is to be understood accordingly, and ﴿hadhani la-sahirani﴾ is a subject and predicate." See also Zad al-Masir, 5/399.]] It is narrated that a Bedouin asked Ibn al-Zubayr for something and he refused it. The man said, "May Allah curse the she-camel that carried me to you!" Ibn al-Zubayr said, "*Inna*, and its companion," meaning "yes."

The poet [[He is 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat. See al-Qurtubi, 11/218.]] said:

*My blaming women rose up against me, reproaching me, and I reproached them back.*
*They said, "Gray hair has come upon you, and you have grown old," and I said, "Inna," [meaning "yes"].*

That is, "yes."

﴿They want to expel you from your land﴾, Egypt [[Omitted in B.]], ﴿by their magic, and to take away your ideal way of life﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning by the noblest of your people and your notables. It is said: "These are the way (*tariqah*) of their people," meaning their nobles [[al-Tabari, 16/183.]]. ﴿Al-Muthla*﴾ is the feminine of *al-amthal*, which means the best. A hadith of al-Sha'bi from 'Ali: "They turn the faces of the people toward them" [[al-Tabari, 16/183.]].

Qatadah said: "Their ideal way of life on that day was the Children of Israel, who were the most numerous of the people in number and wealth. So the enemy of Allah said: 'They want to take them away for themselves.'" [[al-Tabari, 16/183.]]

*Indeed her father, and her father's father,*
*Have both reached the furthest limit in glory.*

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 64–67:

﴿So gather your scheme⟩. Abu 'Amr recited "fa-jma'u" (فَاجْمَعُوا) with a connected alif and a fatha on the mim, from al-jam' (gathering), meaning: leave nothing of your scheme behind except that you bring it, as evidenced by His saying: "then he gathered his scheme" (فَجَمَعَ كَيْدَهُ). **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil, Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 68–72:**

﴿We said﴾ to Musa: ﴿Do not fear. Indeed, you are the superior﴾, meaning the victorious. That is, victory and triumph are yours.

﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾, meaning the staff, ﴿it will swallow﴾, meaning it will seize and swallow, ﴿what they have made﴾. Ibn 'Amir read "talquf" (تَلْقُفُ) here with a raised *fa'* (رفع الفاء), while the others read it with a *jazm* (جزم), as a response to the imperative. ﴿What they have made is only﴾, meaning that what they have made is ﴿the plot of a sorcerer﴾, that is, a trick of magic. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kaydu sahirin" (كَيْدُ سَاحِرٍ) with a *kasra* on the *sin* and without an *alif*. [[This indicates that the author (may Allah have mercy on him) first explained the verse according to the reading "kayda sahirin", as shown by what follows.]] The others read "sahirin" (سَاحِرٍ), because attributing the plot (kayd) to the agent (al-fa'il) is preferable to attributing it to the act (al-fi'l), although that is not impermissible in the Arabic language (al-'Arabiyyah). ﴿And the sorcerer does not succeed, wherever he comes﴾ from the earth. Ibn 'Abbas said: he does not prosper wherever he is. It was also said: its meaning is wherever he resorts to cunning.

﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa." He said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief﴾, meaning your leader and your teacher, ﴿who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾, that is, upon the trunks of palm trees. [[As the poet (Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil al-Yashkuri) said:
"They crucified the Abdi on a palm trunk,
so let not the people of Shayban sneeze except with a sneeze of the trunk."
That is, on the trunk of a palm tree. It is said "in the trunks" (فِي جُذُوعِ) because the one crucified on a wooden post is raised along its length, and then he is placed upon it, so it is said: he was crucified upon it. See the tafsir of al-Tabari: 16/188.]] ﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾, meaning: is it I, regarding your belief in him, or the Lord of Musa, regarding abandoning belief in him? ﴿And more lasting﴾, that is, more enduring.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the magicians: ﴿We will never prefer you﴾, meaning we will never choose you, ﴿over what has come to us of the clear proofs﴾.

Meaning the evidences. Muqatil said: meaning the white hand and the staff.

It was also said: their reasoning was that they said, "If this were magic, where are our ropes and our staffs?"

It was also said: ﴿of the clear proofs﴾ means from the clarification (al-tabyin) and knowledge.

It is related from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah that he said: when they were thrown down prostrate, they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell, and saw the reward of their people, and saw their places in Paradise. At that moment they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over what has come to us of the clear proofs﴾. ﴿And He who created us﴾, that is: we will never prefer you over Allah, who created us. It was also said that this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾, that is: do what you will do. ﴿You can only decide concerning this worldly life﴾, that is: your command and your authority are in this world, and it will soon pass away.

[[As the poet (Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil al-Yashkuri) said:
"They crucified the Abdi on a palm trunk,
so let not the people of Shayban sneeze except with a sneeze of the trunk."
That is, on the trunk of a palm tree. It is said "in the trunks" (فِي جُذُوعِ) because the one crucified on a wooden post is raised along its length, and then he is placed upon it, so it is said: he was crucified upon it. See the tafsir of al-Tabari: 16/188.]] ﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾, meaning: is it I, regarding your belief in him, or the Lord of Musa, regarding abandoning belief in him? ﴿And more lasting﴾, that is, more enduring.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the magicians: ﴿We will never prefer you﴾, meaning we will never choose you, ﴿over what has come to us of the clear proofs﴾.

Meaning the evidences. Muqatil said: meaning the white hand and the staff.

It was also said: their reasoning was that they said, "If this were magic, where are our ropes and our staffs?"

It was also said: ﴿of the clear proofs﴾ means from the clarification (al-tabyin) and knowledge.

It is related from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah that he said: when they were thrown down prostrate, they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell, and saw the reward of their people, and saw their places in Paradise. At that moment they said: ﴿We will never prefer you over what has come to us of the clear proofs﴾. ﴿And He who created us﴾, that is: we will never prefer you over Allah, who created us. It was also said that this is an oath. ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾, that is: do what you will do. ﴿You can only decide concerning this worldly life﴾, that is: your command and your authority are in this world, and it will soon pass away.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins and what you compelled us to do of magic.﴾ If it is asked: How did they say this, when they came choosing (freely), swearing by the might of Pharaoh that they would have the victory?

It is said: It is related from al-Hasan that he said: Pharaoh used to compel a people to learn magic so that his own origin (lineage or foundation of power) would not perish, and he had compelled them at the beginning.

Muqatil said: The magicians were seventy-two: two of them were from the Copts and seventy from the Children of Israel. Pharaoh had compelled those who were from the Children of Israel to learn magic, and that is their saying: ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic﴾.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Aban said: The magicians said to Pharaoh: "Show us Musa when he sleeps." So he showed them Musa sleeping while his staff was guarding him. They said to Pharaoh: "This is not a magician; indeed, when a magician sleeps his magic is nullified." But he refused them anything except that they should learn (magic). That is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic﴾.

﴿And Allah is better and more enduring.﴾ Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Better than you in reward, and more enduring in punishment.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Better than you in reward if He is obeyed, and more enduring than you in punishment if He is disobeyed. This is an answer to his saying: "And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more enduring."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 74–77:

﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal (mujrim) – for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ It is said: this is the beginning of a statement from Allah, the Exalted. ﴿And whoever comes to Him﴾: Abu 'Amr read the hā' (of hu) with sukun (ساكنة الهاء, "with the hā' silent"), and Abu Ja'far and Qalun and Ya'qub read it with khalas (yakhtalisuha, "with a brief, truncated vowel"), while the others read it with ishba' (full vowel, "with the vowel lengthened"). ﴿A believer (mu'minan)﴾ who dies in faith, ﴿who has done righteous deeds – for them are the high ranks (al-darajat al-'ula)﴾, meaning the lofty ranks. ﴿Al-'ula﴾ is the plural, and "al-'ulya" is the feminine form of "al-a'la" (the highest).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 78–81:

﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers.﴾ *Fa-atba'ahum* means that he overtook them. ﴿Pharaoh with his soldiers﴾. It was said: the meaning is that Pharaoh ordered his soldiers to follow Musa and his people, and the *ba'* in *bi-junudihi* is extra (*za'idah*), and he was among them. ﴿Then the sea covered them﴾ means it reached them. ﴿What covered them of the sea﴾ is drowning.

[It was said: *ghashiyahum* means it went over them and covered them, some of the water of the sea, not all of it.] [[Addition from manuscript "B".]]

It was also said: ﴿what covered them of the sea﴾ means the people of Musa, so that he drowned them, and Musa and his people were saved.

﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them﴾, that is, he did not guide them to right direction. This is a refutation of Pharaoh's words: ﴿And I only show you the way of right guidance﴾ (Ghafir 40:29).

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy﴾, Pharaoh, ﴿and We made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount, and We sent down upon you manna and quails﴾. ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you.﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *anjaynakum*, *wa-'adnakum* and *razaqnakum* with the *ta'* (first person singular), indicating oneness. The others recited them with *nun* and *alif*, indicating majesty. They did not differ over *wa-nazzalna*, because it is written with an *alif*.

﴿And do not transgress therein﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: do not wrong (*la tazlimu*). Al-Kalbi said: do not be ungrateful for the blessing, for then you would become transgressors (*taghin*).

It was said: do not spend in disobedience to Me.

It was said: do not hoard, lest you hoard and it spoils (*fatadawwada*).

﴿Lest there descend (*fayahilla*)﴾: al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i recited *fayahulla* with a *damma* on the *ha'*, and *wa-man yahlul* with a *damma* on the *lam*, meaning "descend" (*yanzil*). The others recited it with a *kasra* on the *ha'*, meaning "become due" (*yajib*). ﴿Upon you will be My wrath, and whoever has My wrath descend upon him, then he has certainly fallen﴾, that is, he has perished and plunged into the Fire.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 20, verses 86–87:**

﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieving.﴾ *Hazinan* (grieving).

﴿He said, "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"﴾ *Sidqan* (a true promise): that He would give you the Torah. ﴿Has the time seemed long to you?﴾ That is, the period of my separation from you. ﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord would descend upon you?﴾ n. That is: did you wish to do an action that would make wrath from your Lord obligatory upon you? ﴿So you broke your promise to me.﴾

﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will."﴾ *Bi-mulkina* was recited by Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Asim with a *fatha* on the *mim*. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a *damma* on the *mim*. The others recited it with a *kasra* on the *mim*. The meaning of the *kasra* reading is: "while we were in control of our affair." It is also said: "by our choice." Whoever recited with the *damma* means: "by our power and authority." This is because a person who falls into trial and temptation does not control himself.

﴿But we were made to carry﴾: Abu Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub recited *hamalna* with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and a light *mim*. The others recited *hummilna* with a *damma* on the *ha'* and a doubled *mim*. The meaning is: they made us carry them, and we were burdened with carrying them. ﴿the burdens of the people's adornments﴾: that is, the ornaments of the people of Pharaoh. He called them *awzar* (burdens) because they had taken them by way of loan (*ariyah*) and did not return them. This is because the children of Israel had borrowed ornaments from the Copts, and these were with them when they left Egypt.

It is also said that when Allah the Exalted drowned Pharaoh, the sea cast up their ornaments, and they took them. They were regarded as spoils, and spoils were not lawful for them in that era. So He called them *awzar* for this reason.

﴿Then we threw them﴾: it is said that the Samiri told them, "Dig a pit and throw them into it until Musa returns."

Al-Suddi said: Harun said to them, "Those are spoils that are not lawful. So dig a pit and throw them into it until Musa returns, and he will see his opinion regarding them." So they did. (*Source: al-Tabari, 16/200.*) His words ﴿we threw them﴾ mean: we cast them into the pit.

﴿Thus the Samiri cast﴾ what he had of the ornaments into it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Harun lit a fire and said, "Throw into it whatever you have with you." So they threw it in. Then the Samiri cast in what he had of the dust from the hoofprint of Jibril's horse. (*Source: al-Tabari, 16/201.*)

Qatadah said: He had taken a handful of that dust and kept it in his turban.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verses 88–91:

﴿So he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot."﴾ That is: Moses left it here and went off seeking Him. It was also said: he took the wrong path and went astray [[See: al-Tabari: 16/201.]]. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them any word, and that it possesses no harm or benefit for them?﴾ That is: do they not see that the calf does not speak to them and does not answer them when they call upon it? It was also said: Harun passed by al-Samiri while he was shaping the calf, and said to him: "What is this?" He said: "I am making something that benefits and does no harm, so pray for me." Harun said: "O Allah, give him what he asked of You according to what is in his heart." So he put dust into the mouth of the calf and said: "Be a calf that lows," and it was so, by the supplication of Harun [[For what has preceded: 5/271, takhrij of the hadith of "al-Futun"; and see Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/163.]].

And the reality is that this was a trial with which Allah tested the Children of Israel.

﴿And Harun had already said to them before this﴾ before the return of Moses, ﴿"O my people, you are only being tested by it,"﴾ you were tried with the calf, ﴿"and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me"﴾ in my religion of worshipping Allah, ﴿"and obey my command"﴾ in abandoning the worship of the calf.

﴿They said, "We will not cease﴾ that is, we will not stop, ﴿"devoted to it"﴾ to its worship, ﴿"remaining"﴾ abiding, ﴿"until Moses returns to us."﴾ So Harun separated himself from them along with twelve thousand of those who had not worshipped the calf. When Moses returned and heard the shouting and clamour, and they were dancing around the calf, he said to the seventy who were with him: "This is the sound of the trial." When Harun saw this, he seized his head by its hair with his right hand and his beard with his left.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 92–96:

﴿He said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,"﴾ i.e., associating partners with Allah.

﴿"from following me?"﴾ Meaning: [why did you not follow me], and "lā" is extra (ṣilah), i.e., "that you follow my command and my instruction." The meaning is: "Why did you not fight them, when you knew that if I had been among them I would have fought them over their disbelief?"

It is also said: "an lā tattabiʿanī" means: "What prevented you from joining me and informing me of their misguidance, so that your separation from them would be a deterrent to them from what they had committed?" ﴿"Did you then disobey my command?"﴾ i.e., did you oppose my command?

﴿He said: "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or by my head."﴾ i.e., by the hair of my head, and he had taken hold of its locks. ﴿"Indeed, I feared"﴾ that if I had denounced them, they would have split into two factions, killing one another, ﴿"that you would say, 'You have divided the Children of Israel'"﴾ i.e., I feared that if I separated from them and followed you, they would become factions fighting one another, and you would say, "You have divided the Children of Israel."[[al-Tabari mentions in his tafsir (16/204) other sayings in addition to what the author mentioned, and he preferred what is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: that Musa rebuked his brother Harun for not following his command with those among the believers who had followed him. Harun said to him: "I feared that you would say: 'You have separated their community,' so I left some of them behind me and brought some of them with me." See also Zad al-Masir: 5/316.]] ﴿"and you did not observe my word."﴾ i.e., you did not keep my instruction when I said to you: "Take my place among my people, and set things right," i.e., deal gently with them.[[See: al-Tabari: 16/204; al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/596.]]

Then Musa turned to the Samiri: ﴿He said: "What is your affair?"﴾ i.e., what is your situation and concern? And what moved you to do what you did? ﴿"O Samiri?"﴾

﴿He said: "I saw what they did not see"﴾ i.e., I saw what they did not see, and I recognized what they did not recognize.

Hamzah and al-Kisai read "mā lam tabṣurū" with the "tā" in the second person (address), while the others read it with the "yā" in the third person (report).

﴿"So I seized a handful from the footprint of the Messenger"﴾ i.e., from the dust of the footprint of Jibril's horse. ﴿"and threw it"﴾ i.e., I cast it into the mouth of the calf.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 97:

﴿He said, "Then go, for indeed, for you in [this] life"﴾ means: as long as you are alive, ﴿that you will say, "No contact"﴾ means: do not mix with anyone, and let no one mix with you. Moses commanded the Children of Israel that they should not mix with him or approach him.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "No contact for you and for your offspring." The word "al-misas" (contact) derives from "al-mumassah" (touching), meaning: none of us should touch another. So the Samiri wandered in the wilderness with the wild beasts and predators, touching no one and no one touching him. God punished him with this, and whenever he met anyone he would say, "No contact," meaning: do not come near me and do not touch me.

It is also said: whenever he touched someone or someone touched him, both of them would be struck with fever together, so much so that their descendants today still say this, and whenever someone from other than them touches one of them, both are struck with fever at once [[See: al-Qurtubi: 11/241; Zad al-Masir: 5/319.]].

﴿And indeed for you﴾ O Samiri, ﴿is an appointment﴾ for your punishment, ﴿which you will not fail to meet.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿lan tukhlafahu﴾ with a kasra on the lam, meaning: you will not be absent from it, and you will have no escape from it, but you will meet it on the Day of Resurrection. The others read it with a fatha on the lam, meaning: you will not deny it, and God will not break it for you. Its meaning is that God Most High will recompense you for your deed, and you will not escape it [[Mentioned by al-Tabari, both readings: 16/206-207, and he said: "The view I hold is that they are two well-known readings, close in meaning, because there is no doubt that God fulfils His promise to His creatures, gathering them to the station of reckoning, and that creatures will all meet that Day; so God will not break that for them, nor will they break their absence from it. Whichever of the two readers recites, he is correct in that."]].

﴿And look at your god﴾ according to your claim, ﴿to which you remained devoted﴾ meaning: you continued and kept persisting in worshipping it. The Arabs say "zaltu af'alu kadhha" meaning "ziltu", and "mistu" meaning "massastu".

﴿We will surely burn it﴾ with fire. Abu Ja'far read it with a lightened form from "al-ihraq" (burning). ﴿Then we will surely scatter it﴾ we will winnow it away, ﴿into the sea﴾ into the sea, ﴿a scattering.﴾ It is narrated that Moses took the calf, slaughtered it, and blood flowed from it, because it had become flesh and blood; then he burned it with fire, then scattered it into the sea [[See: al-Durr al-Manthur 5/597; al-Qurtubi: 11/242-243.]]. Ibn Muhaysin read "lanahruqannahu" with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the ra', meaning "we will file it down with a file," and from this the file is called "al-muhriq." Al-Suddi said: Moses took the calf, slaughtered it, then burned it with a file, then scattered it into the sea.

﴿Thus do We relate to you some news of what has passed﴾ of the matters, ﴿and We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ meaning the Qur'an.

﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾ i.e., from the Qur'an, by not believing in it and not acting upon what is in it, ﴿indeed, he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾ a heavy load of sin.

﴿Abiding therein﴾ remaining in the punishment of the burden, ﴿and evil is it for them on the Day of Resurrection as a load﴾ (14/a) i.e., how evil is what they loaded upon themselves of sin, by disbelieving in the Qur'an.
